Pelvic & Acetabular Trauma · Chapter 51

Fractures of the Acetabulum

A surgeon's reference to the Letournel–Judet classification, surgical approaches, and operative management — synthesized from Rockwood & Green (10e) and the AO Foundation Surgery Reference.

Source · R&G 10e Ch. 51 Author · Gary & Phelps Incidence · ~3 / 100,000 / year Classification · Letournel (10 patterns)
§ 1 / 7

Overview

Acetabular fractures arise from force transmitted through the femoral head to the articular surface. Incidence has been stable at ~3 per 100,000 / year for four decades, but the population is aging — a bimodal distribution now spans young high-energy trauma and elderly low-energy falls.

Epidemiology

  • Bimodal distribution: young adulthood (high-energy MVC, fall from height) and later decades (osteopenic, low-energy fall on greater trochanter)
  • Most common operative patterns: posterior wall, transverse + posterior wall, both-column
  • Both-column is the most common pattern in the elderly
  • Regional incidence varies with population demographics and proximity to high-speed roadways

Goals of Treatment

Central principle

The goal of treatment is to obtain a stable and concentric reduction of the hip joint until bony healing has occurred. For displaced fractures, this requires anatomic reduction (<2 mm residual displacement) of the articular surface — particularly the weight-bearing dome.

Associated Injuries

Other musculoskeletal/visceral injuries occur in >50% of high-energy cases. Even elderly low-energy fractures have ~30% associated injuries. ATLS protocol always applies.

  • Knee — dashboard injuries (PCL, meniscus, bone bruise) often missed initially; up to 15% have ipsilateral knee symptoms within 1 year
  • Sciatic nerve — injured in up to 30%; usually partial, peroneal division most often affected
  • Pelvic ring — combined injuries in ~9% of acetabular fractures; affect hemodynamics and reduction strategy
  • Femoral head / neck — femoral neck fracture in physiologically young patient is a surgical emergency
  • Morel–Lavallé lesion — closed degloving; small (≤50 mL) can be aspirated, larger may require formal debridement

Initial Reduction Priorities

Emergent operative indications
  • Recurrent dislocation despite traction
  • Irreducible hip dislocation
  • Progressive sciatic nerve deficit after fracture or closed reduction
  • Associated vascular injury requiring repair
  • Open fractures
  • Ipsilateral femoral neck fracture

Key Historical Context

Judet et al. (1964) brought clarity with the first systematic radiographic classification. Letournel and Judet (1981, 1993) refined the system and surgical approaches that remain the gold standard. Matta later disseminated these principles globally and emphasized the <2 mm anatomic reduction standard.

§ 2 / 7

Anatomy

The acetabulum sits at the convergence of pubis, ischium, and ilium — three bones fused at the triradiate cartilage. Letournel's column concept reframed this region: the articular surface rests between two limbs of an inverted Y, linked superiorly to the sacrum by the sciatic buttress.

The Two-Column Concept

The innominate bone supports the acetabulum via an inverted Y of bone — anterior and posterior columns meeting at the acetabular dome. These columns connect to the sacrum through the sciatic buttress, a thick strut above the greater sciatic notch.

The plane of the ilium is approximately 90° to the obturator foramen, and both are oriented ~45° to the frontal plane — the rationale behind the standard 45° oblique radiographic views.

Anterior Column

Anterior half of the iliac wing → pelvic brim → superior pubic ramus. Includes anterior half of acetabular articular surface and the anterior wall.

Posterior Column

Begins at superior aspect of greater sciatic notch → contiguous with greater and lesser sciatic notches → ischial tuberosity. Includes the posterior wall.

Quadrilateral Plate

Internal cortical surface of acetabulum where the two columns meet. Common site of rotational displacement; correction is critical.

The Weight-Bearing Dome

Functionally critical region

The superior portion of the acetabular articular surface — the "dome" or "roof" — extends from just posterior to the AIIS to the superior aspect of the posterior column. Fracture displacement through this region must be anatomically reduced, as it bears the primary load at mid-stance (vector is 16° medial from vertical).

Critical Soft Tissue Relationships

Blood Supply

External Acetabulum

  • Superior gluteal artery (dominant)
  • Inferior gluteal artery
  • Obturator artery
  • Medial femoral circumflex artery

Internal Acetabulum

  • 4th lumbar artery
  • Iliolumbar artery (main nutrient to ilium → supra-acetabular)
  • Obturator artery

Posterior Wall

Branches of superior and inferior gluteal arteries — capsular attachments to PW fragments must be preserved.

The Medial Femoral Circumflex Artery

Femoral head blood supply — protect at all costs

The deep branch of the MFCA is the dominant blood supply to the femoral head. It is protected by the obturator externus tendon. Disruption of this tendon — by trauma or surgery — places the head's blood supply at great risk.

Surgical implication

Transect piriformis and obturator internus tendons at least 1.5 cm from greater trochanter to avoid the ascending branch of the MFCA. Avoid dissection caudal to the inferior gemellus on the femoral side. Elevate quadratus femoris from its ischial attachment, not femoral, if more distal exposure is needed.

§ 3 / 7

Imaging

Letournel's classification was derived by analyzing radiographic landmarks of the intact dry innominate bone, then correlating disruption of those "lines" with fracture morphology. Modern CT (especially 3D reconstruction) supplements but does not replace fluency with plain films — fluoroscopy still drives intraoperative reduction.

Standard Radiographic Series

Three views are obtained for any suspected acetabular fracture: AP pelvis, obturator oblique (45° internal / hemipelvis rotated 45° toward beam), and iliac oblique (45° external / hemipelvis rotated 45° away from beam).

AP Pelvis — 6 Lines

  1. Iliopectineal line — anterior column
  2. Ilioischial line — posterior column
  3. Radiographic U / teardrop
  4. Acetabular roof
  5. Anterior rim — anterior wall
  6. Posterior rim — posterior wall

Obturator Oblique

Hemipelvis rotated 45° toward beam. Coccyx lies above ipsilateral femoral head.

Best for: posterior wall, anterior column, obturator foramen en face

Iliac Oblique

Hemipelvis rotated 45° away from beam. Coccyx lies above contralateral femoral head.

Best for: posterior column, iliac wing en face, anterior rim

The 6 AP Landmarks — What They Represent

LineAnatomic originFracture implication
IliopectinealAnterior ¾ = pelvic brim; posterior ¼ = sciatic buttress cortexAnterior column disruption
IlioischialTangency to posterior quadrilateral surfacePosterior column disruption
Radiographic U / teardropMedial limb: obturator canal + anteroinferior quadrilateral; lateral limb: inferior anterior wall + cotyloid fossaNormally superimposed on ilioischial line — dissociation = hemipelvis rotation or quadrilateral plate fracture
RoofSubchondral bone tangency, superior acetabulumDisruption = articular surface fracture
Anterior rimAnterior wall lateral marginHas characteristic undulation; typically medial to posterior rim
Posterior rimPosterior wall lateral marginMore vertical than anterior rim; contiguous inferiorly with posterior horn condensation

Recognizing Posterior Hip Dislocation on AP

Subtle radiographic signs
  • Break in Shenton's line
  • Proximal migration of the lesser trochanter
  • Affected femoral head appears smaller (closer to x-ray cassette)
  • Bony double density above the femoral head (posterior wall fragment sitting atop dislocated head)

The double density often gives the appearance of a normal joint space — a common cause of missed diagnosis.

CT Scan — Essential Adjunct

  • Sections ≤3 mm contiguous
  • Superior to plain films for fracture step-off and gap measurements
  • Identifies: marginal impaction, intra-articular fragments, femoral head injury, fracture line orientation, hidden T-component / quadrilateral plate fragments, rotation, pelvic ring injuries
  • 2D CT can measure posterior wall fragment size — but does not reliably predict hip stability
  • 3D reconstructions and "ghost" CT-derived Judet views increasingly replace painful repositioning for oblique films

Fracture Orientation on Axial CT

CT line orientation pearl
  • Both columns / one column — coronal or sagittal-oriented line
  • Transverse — anterior-to-posterior oriented line
  • Anterior wall — fracture line on anterior side
  • Posterior wall — fracture line on posterior side

Dynamic Stress Examination Under Anesthesia

Moed's described technique remains the most reliable test for hip stability in posterior wall fractures, where static imaging is unreliable:

  • Patient supine, C-arm from ipsilateral side for obturator oblique view
  • Hip flexed past 90°, adducted, internally rotated, with posterior-directed axial load along femur
  • For cranial PW fractures: also test in extension/adduction/axial load
  • Do NOT redislocate the hip — neither necessary nor desirable
  • Positive: widening medial joint space or loss of joint parallelism = dynamic instability
§ 4 / 7

Classification

The Letournel classification — refined from Judet's 1964 original — defines 10 fracture patterns: 5 elementary (single column or part of a column) and 5 associated (combinations or elementary + additional component). It remains the international language of acetabular surgery despite the AO/OTA Type 62 alphanumeric overlay.

Interactive Classification Explorer

Tap any pattern to view its incidence, mechanism, radiographic findings, key distinguishing features, and preferred approach.

Distinguishing the Difficult Ones

Posterior Wall vs Posterior Column

Both disrupt the posterior rim — but PC also disrupts the ilioischial line. PW shows posterior rim broken in TWO locations (defining the articular fragment); PC shows posterior rim broken in ONE location where the column fracture crosses it.

Anterior Wall vs Very-Low Anterior Column

Both can disrupt the iliopectineal line near the eminence. The very-low AC has a fracture of the inferior pubic ramus and a single break in the iliopectineal line. The classic anterior wall (Letournel description) has two breaks in the iliopectineal line.

Transverse vs T-Shaped vs Both-Column

  • Transverse: both columns disrupted, but ilioischial line maintains its normal relation to teardrop. Ischial ramus NOT fractured.
  • T-shaped: Transverse + ischial ramus fracture. Stem may extend through ischiopubic ramus, ischium, or near pubic body.
  • Both-column: NO articular surface remains attached to the axial skeleton. "Spur sign" on obturator oblique is pathognomonic. Anterior and posterior columns split.
The "spur sign"

A bony spike representing the caudal external cortex of the intact ilium, visible because the entire articular surface has medialized away from it. Best seen on obturator oblique. Pathognomonic for associated both-column fracture.

The "Gull Wing" Sign

Subgroups of the Elementary Patterns

Posterior Column + Posterior Wall

AO/OTA Type 62 Classification Overlay

The 2018 AO/OTA classification organizes the same Letournel patterns alphanumerically. Recognition of either system is essential, but Letournel terminology remains dominant in operative communication.

§ 5 / 7

Management

Treatment is driven by joint stability, congruity, and dome involvement — modified by patient age, bone quality, and demands. The 2 mm rule for residual displacement remains the operative threshold for the weight-bearing dome.

Nonoperative Indications

  • Stable nondisplaced or minimally displaced fractures
  • Intact acetabulum maintains stability AND congruity:
    • Caudal anterior column, caudal transverse, caudal T-shaped fractures
    • Both-column fractures with secondary congruence
    • Wall fractures not compromising hip stability
  • Infirm patients unable to withstand surgery
  • Severe osteoporosis precluding adequate fixation (lower demand)

Roof Arc Measurements (Matta)

Measured on each of the three views with femoral head concentrically reduced (no traction): vertical line through femoral head center; second line from center to fracture exit at articular surface.

ViewRoof arcThreshold (original)Updated (Vrahas)
APMedial roof arc>45°>45°
Obturator obliqueAnterior roof arc>45°>25°
Iliac obliquePosterior roof arc>45°>70°
Caveats

Roof arcs are NOT applicable to both-column fractures (no intact acetabulum to measure) or posterior wall fractures (intact dome above the wall fragment). For PW, dynamic stress exam is the reliable test.

Operative Indications

  • Hip instability (obvious or demonstrated on exam under anesthesia)
  • Joint incongruity from displacement in weight-bearing dome
  • Intra-articular bone or soft tissue fragments
  • Loss of parallelism between femoral head and acetabular articular surface on any of the three Judet views
  • >2 mm residual displacement in weight-bearing dome (failed roof arc criteria)

Timing of Surgery

  • Most cases are not emergent — optimize medically first
  • Avoid delay beyond 15 days for elementary patterns, 10 days for associated
  • Anatomic reduction odds decrease ~12% per day from injury
  • Beyond 10 days: early fracture healing limits fragment mobility
  • Beyond 2 weeks: more extensive approach often required (transverse, T-shaped, AC+PHT, both-column)
  • Beyond 3 weeks: callus formation makes injury "non-acute"

Geriatric Considerations

The aging acetabulum population
  • 2.4× increase in elderly acetabular fractures from 1980 → 2007
  • Predominant patterns: anterior column, AC + posterior hemitransverse, both-column
  • Define elderly by physiologic age, not chronologic
  • Primary goal shifts: preserve life, mobilize early, minimize narcotic dependence — preserve native hip is secondary
  • Options: nonoperative, ORIF (open or percutaneous), acute THA
  • Nondisplaced/minimally displaced: 7% progress to significant displacement; 94% retain native hip at 10 years
  • Step-off <2 mm on obturator oblique: safe nonoperative management
  • Acute THA factors (Tannast nomogram): age >40, anterior dislocation, femoral head cartilage lesion, PW involvement, marginal impaction, initial displacement >20 mm, non-anatomic reduction, postop incongruence, extended iliofemoral use

Outcome Measures

Historically: modified Merle d'Aubigné and Postel score (pain + walking + ROM, 18 = excellent). Now supplemented by validated patient-reported measures (PROMIS, SMFA, SF-36). Survivorship of the native hip (conversion to THA or arthrodesis) is increasingly used as a hard outcome.

Authors' Preferred — ORIF Posterior Wall Step Walkthrough

Posterior wall is the most common operative pattern. Walk through the key surgical steps:

General Fracture Reduction Sequence

Reduction order

For most fractures: reduce and stabilize displaced columns first → reduce impacted osteochondral fragments and backfill metaphyseal void → reduce any wall fracture.

For both-column: reduce and stabilize one column (usually anterior) to the axial skeleton → then the other column → then the wall component (if large enough to require fixation).

Anatomic Reduction Definition

<2 mm residual displacement (Letournel/Matta). Standard plate and screw constructs (requiring open surgery) have demonstrated greater yield strength and maximal load at failure than percutaneous counterparts. Open ORIF remains the mainstay for displaced fractures.

Surgical Approaches

Selection of approach is one of the most important pre-op decisions — driven by fracture type, time from injury, and location of maximal displacement. The single-approach principle (with sequential combinations when needed) has largely supplanted extended approaches.

PatternPreferred approach
Posterior wallKocher–Langenbeck (prone or lateral)
Posterior columnKocher–Langenbeck (prone preferred)
Anterior wallIlioinguinal (or modified Smith-Petersen for AW variant)
Anterior columnIlioinguinal or modified Stoppa ± lateral window; iliofemoral for high variants
TransverseK-L if posterior dominant; ilioinguinal/Stoppa if anterior
Posterior column + PWKocher–Langenbeck
Transverse + PWKocher–Langenbeck (most often)
AC + posterior hemitransverseIlioinguinal or modified Stoppa ± lateral window
T-shapedK-L if posterior dominant; combined or extended iliofemoral for transtectal/wide stem
Both-column (associated)Ilioinguinal or modified Stoppa; combined if displaced PC or SI extension
Kocher–Langenbeck

Kocher–Langenbeck (Posterior)

The workhorse approach for posterior pathology. Provides direct visualization of the entire lateral aspect of the posterior column. Indirect access (palpating finger, special instruments through greater sciatic notch) to the quadrilateral surface. Posterior capsulotomy gives limited joint access — usually unnecessary in the presence of a PW fracture.

K-L Step Walkthrough

Ilioinguinal

Ilioinguinal (Anterior)

Access to the internal aspect of the innominate bone from SI joint to symphysis pubis. Three "windows" defined by retracting key structures.

The Three Windows

Lateral Window

Created by subperiosteal elevation of iliacus from internal iliac fossa.

Exposes: iliac crest, internal iliac fossa medially to SI joint, distally to pelvic brim.

Middle Window

Created by releasing iliopectineal fascia and retracting iliopsoas/femoral nerve laterally, external iliac vessels medially.

Exposes: anterior wall, pectineal eminence, pelvic brim, quadrilateral surface.

Medial Window

Created by retracting external iliac vessels laterally with spermatic cord/round ligament medial or lateral. Rectus abdominis tendon may be transected.

Exposes: space of Retzius, superior pubic ramus, pubic symphysis.

Corona Mortis

Structures at risk — ilioinguinal
  • Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve — protect or excise 2 cm prophylactically (discuss with patient pre-op)
  • External iliac artery/vein — check pulse frequently; thrombosis from prolonged retraction
  • Femoral nerve — within iliopsoas, in middle window
  • Inguinal canal contents — spermatic cord / round ligament
  • Sciatic nerve — can be injured by posteriorly directed drill or screw despite anterior approach
Modified Stoppa (Anterior Intrapelvic)

Modified Stoppa Intrapelvic Approach

No longer truly "alternative" — now arguably the most common anterior approach. Used in conjunction with the lateral window of the ilioinguinal, or alone. Transverse incision 2 cm above symphysis, dissection through linea alba, extraperitoneal access.

  • Advantages: improved access to quadrilateral surface and posterior column; avoids middle window of ilioinguinal (no iliac vessel dissection)
  • Indications: anterior wall, AC, transverse, T-shaped, AC + posterior hemitransverse, both-column fractures; especially useful for quadrilateral plate buttress plating and gull-sign impaction
  • Approach trend: younger surgeons increasingly favor Stoppa + lateral window over classic ilioinguinal — many fellows complete training without seeing full ilioinguinal
  • Obturator nerve injury: 26% in one series (Stoppa); usually resolves <12 months
  • Sciatic nerve at risk from retractors in sciatic notch / along inferior quadrilateral plate
Iliofemoral

Iliofemoral Approach

Limited applications. Provides intrapelvic access to iliac crest and entire internal iliac fossa, but cannot reach medial to iliopectineal eminence.

  • Best for high anterior column fractures with main displacement cephalad to hip joint
  • Patient supine on standard radiolucent table (NOT fracture table — limb prepped free, hip flexed 60–90°, adducted)
  • Limited indirect access to true pelvis (finger or instrument as far as superior quadrilateral plate)
  • LFCN commonly injured — typical, accept
Extended Iliofemoral

Extended Iliofemoral

Rarely used in the 21st century — high complication rate (infection 4–19%, HO, decreased hip motion) and unfamiliarity. Almost exclusively reserved for delayed treatment of associated fracture types where fracture healing precludes indirect manipulation.

  • Patient in lateral position
  • Inverted J incision: PSIS → iliac crest → ASIS → midline thigh, angling toward 2 cm lateral to patella
  • Provides maximum simultaneous access to BOTH columns
  • Hip kept extended, knee flexed to relax sciatic nerve
Alternative

Trochanteric Flip Osteotomy

Variation of K-L (or modified Gibson) for additional anterosuperior exposure and surgical dislocation of the femoral head for joint inspection. The "digastric" osteotomy keeps abductor + vastus lateralis insertions on the trochanteric fragment, with piriformis remaining on the intact proximal femur — protecting the deep branch of the MFCA.

  • Indications: combined femoral head + PW fractures, complex PW/PC, certain transverse/T-shaped
  • Lateral patient position required if surgical dislocation planned
  • Cadaveric studies: visualization improves but actual access to relevant superior acetabulum may not differ from K-L alone

Modified Gibson

Differs from K-L by using the interval between gluteus maximus and tensor fasciae latae rather than splitting the gluteus maximus. Preserves anterior gluteus maximus innervation. Straight (rather than angled) incision is more cosmetically appealing in obese female patients. Often used with trochanteric flip osteotomy.

Combined Anterior + Posterior

Sequential (preferred) or simultaneous (rarely used). Indicated for AC + posterior hemitransverse, T-shaped, both-column, or transverse + PW patterns where a single approach proves insufficient. Maximize skin bridge, avoid undermining. Simultaneous lateral positioning often compromises both exposures — sequential is generally preferred over simultaneous or extended iliofemoral.

§ 7 / 7

Complications

The complexity of acetabular surgery — bony, neurovascular, and durational — yields a substantial complication profile. Anticipation and prevention dominate management; once established, many of these complications materially worsen outcome.

Post-Traumatic Arthritis

  • Most important predictor of outcome
  • Driven by: residual articular displacement (>2 mm), marginal impaction, femoral head cartilage damage, intra-articular hardware, late reduction
  • Step-off >2 mm on obturator oblique view = strongest predictor of poor clinical outcome and need for THA
  • Conversion to THA used as a survivorship endpoint

Osteonecrosis of the Femoral Head

MFCA preservation principles
  • Transect short external rotators ≥1.5 cm from greater trochanter (ascending branch of MFCA)
  • Do NOT dissect caudal to inferior gemellus on the femoral side
  • Elevate quadratus femoris from ischial insertion, not femoral, if more distal exposure needed
  • Trochanteric flip osteotomy preserves MFCA — piriformis stays on intact proximal femur
  • Avoid posterior capsulotomy unless necessary

Infection

  • Extended iliofemoral has historically reported infection 4–19% — drives away from this approach
  • Embolization controversy: was thought to increase infection risk; more recent data show similar or lower rates vs no embolization
  • Morel-Lavallé lesion management critical to limiting infection risk
  • Standard approaches have lower rates with careful soft tissue handling

Iatrogenic Nerve Injury

NerveApproach riskMechanismPrevention
SciaticK-L, modified Gibson, extended iliofemoralRetractor pressure, hip flexion + knee extension, fracture fragmentsVisualize from quadratus femoris to greater sciatic notch; hip extension + knee flexion; intermittent retractor relaxation
Superior glutealK-L, extended iliofemoralExcessive superior abductor retraction; entrapped in PC fracture at greater sciatic notchIdentify bundle exiting greater sciatic notch above piriformis; extract from fracture site before reduction
FemoralIlioinguinal middle windowExcessive lateral retraction within iliopsoas massPeriodic relaxation of middle-window retractor
ObturatorModified Stoppa, quadrilateral plate fracturesStretch with hip/knee flexion; direct injury during quadrilateral exposureLocate nerve in operative field (Fig 51-60); 26% palsy in one Stoppa series; most resolve <12 months
Lateral femoral cutaneousIlioinguinal, iliofemoralVariable anatomy near ASISIdentify and protect, or prophylactically excise 2 cm (discuss with patient pre-op)

Venous Thromboembolism

  • Significant risk given polytrauma, immobilization, pelvic vasculature
  • Chemoprophylaxis balanced against fracture-related bleeding
  • IVC filter use in select polytrauma patients with contraindications to anticoagulation (institutional protocol-dependent)

Intra-Articular Hardware

Critical pre-closure check

Confirm extra-articular position of ALL screws on AP, obturator oblique, and iliac oblique fluoroscopic views before leaving the OR. Especially critical for: PW buttress plate fixation, anterior column screws along pelvic brim, posterior column screws from the ischium. Use ROM to detect crepitance.

Heterotopic Ossification

  • Most prevalent complication in posterior approaches
  • Brooker classification (I–IV) for severity
  • Prophylaxis options: NSAIDs (indomethacin), single-fraction radiation (700 cGy within 72 hours)
  • Excision reserved for symptomatic Brooker III/IV with mature lesion (typically 6 months)
  • Antegrade IM nailing of femur (when combined injury) increases HO rates; retrograde nailing has minimal impact on K-L approach

Loss of Reduction

  • Improperly contoured buttress plate → fragment motion → loss of PW fixation
  • Inadequate metaphyseal void backfill → late impaction
  • Inadequate caudal fixation in PW failing with caudal tension force
  • Osteopenia compromising screw purchase — locked plating offers no demonstrated advantage in clinical studies despite biomechanical equivalence

Failure Sequence — Operative Patient Likely to Need Early THA

Tannast 2012 nomogram predictors (within 2 years post-ORIF):

  1. Age >40 years
  2. Anterior dislocation
  3. Femoral head cartilage lesion
  4. Posterior wall involvement
  5. Marginal impaction
  6. Initial displacement >20 mm
  7. Non-anatomic reduction
  8. Postoperative incongruence of acetabular roof
  9. Use of extended iliofemoral approach

Note: the nomogram has not been validated for predicting outcome in isolated posterior wall fractures — clinical judgment required for these.
